utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 1998, did you say that Zoran Zigic has light brown hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly I did, possibly I said that, but I always said that I didn't see him properly and didn't actually take note of what he looked like, so I can't really say. I just heard a voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you cannot state that, then, I would like to point it out in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man didn't come all the time. He wasn't in the camp non-stop, so I couldn't see -- I didn't see him much, and I didn't know him so I don't want to say -- talk about things I don't know. I heard some things, of course. Possibly I had seen him, possibly I saw him, but I wasn't -- I didn't dare look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just asked a direct question. Did you state in that statement of yours, dated 1998, that Zoran Zigic was 40 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly I did say that, but different people came to me and I mixed them up. But as I didn't know him personally, perhaps I did say that, but once again I state I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The individual with light brown hair, did that individual call out Began, Kiki, and Rezak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said, and I remember that there was an individual with brown hair. Now, whether that was Zigic or anybody else. But at one point I heard a voice say "Kiki, Zigic wants you."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you said brown hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but whether that was actually Zigic or another person, I cannot confirm that at this point because I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Kiki did move towards the "white house," as he was called out to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the other two, Rezak and Beganovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I did not know -- I just said I saw Kiki. But whether that happened on that occasion or another occasion, I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Stojanovic. Could you make pauses between your questions and the witness' answers, otherwise we have great difficulty in the interpretation because your voices overlap. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I do apologise, and I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, when the Prosecution showed you a photo spread, did you recognise the individual who called Kiki, Rezak, and Began out and took them off to the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember recognising them, identifying them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will not be tendering an exhibit which has already been tendered by the Prosecution, but I would like to refer to Exhibit 3/83A, B, C, and D, and D1, which was presented yesterday by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that afterwards you only saw Kiki all bloody, coming out of the "white house"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far were you able to see him? How far were you able to watch him walk? Was it in a path in front of the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was lying down so I could see him walk for a metre or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was he then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kiki.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was moving towards the restaurant, on the concrete flower pots.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So he was on the pista, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, behind, because we were lying down on the pista, on the concrete, the asphalt on the pista. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand. Which path are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were flowers. We were on the pista, there were flowers, and he was the other side. I saw him pass the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far away from the "white house" was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite far away, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he alone on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was followed -- escorted by a guard. I saw a number of people. I saw one guard. Who else was there, I don't know. As I say, we were all lying down, and if a guard would notice you looking, he would beat you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to another area. You received a decision on the termination of your employment for your participation in the rebellion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got out of the camp, I went to report to my company and I was told to go to the administrative department to see whether I was on the list for termination of employment. And that's what I got, in fact, this decision whereby my employment was terminated and I was no longer able to go to work. I didn't have a job anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you appeal against that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not protest against the allegation that you had taken part in an armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where I was, where I had come from, I knew what the situation was like. I took the decision and went back home. I feared any consequences. And when I read it, I signed it. I was so afraid that I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you left, did your father stay in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Prijedor, after you left Trnopolje, until April 1993, did you use power and the telephone in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't use the telephone. We had electricity when there was any electricity, but there were power cuts often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in your possession any documents about the fact that you had to sign off your property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I do not have possession of those documents, but my wife brought them to me in Trnopolje for me to be able to leave Trnopolje. I didn't dare carry any other documents when I left for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank the witness, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Hollis, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked questions about the drip that you gave -- that you were given by the detainee doctor. Do you know who gave the doctor that drip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know who gave it to him. But I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know if it was given to him specifically to be used by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know. How he got it, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during cross-examination you were asked if you stayed on the pista for your first month. During direct examination, you said you stayed on the pista more than one month. Can you tell the Court, how long did you stay on the pista? Was it one month or was it longer than one month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For more than one month, but we slept inside. I may have spent 10 to 20 days in the hangar, and then later in Mujo's room, but I spent most of my time on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you were asked today about uniforms that Kvocka wore and you indicated that he wore a police camouflage uniform. Are you able today to remember what other uniforms, if any, Kvocka may have worn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. He may have wore other uniforms but I cannot remember. I can't remember what kind of uniforms people wore, and I wouldn't like to give an incorrect answer. So I just can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked about two men you knew who were beaten, Ismet Okic and Hamdija Brkic. Now, when you were in Omarska, that first night you were there, where were you when you first saw these two men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mujo's dormitory when I saw them for the first time, and they told us that they had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw them in Mujo's room, did you observe any physical signs of beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were swollen, with bloodstains. It was visible. One could see it on their face. Of course I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And I believe you testified they told you they had been beaten at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said. And even if they hadn't said it, it was visible. They were neighbours, they were there together, so he told his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, that night in Mujo's room, were they beaten in Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, they were not, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Also, speaking about Mujo's room, you said that you went into Mujo's room late that night. When you went into Mujo's room, how many people were in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a number of people. I tried to find the best place for myself to be able to sit down. I don't know the exact figure. I couldn't even get to meet all the people in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to move freely in that room that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You sat down and you stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked quite a few questions about the incident where you heard a man calling out names quite loudly, and you were asked what that man was wearing and you said that you didn't look closely. Why didn't you look closely when that man came, yelling out those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of fear. I was afraid that he might call me out too. Whenever people came from the outside, they would call out people, and we were afraid. I didn't know those people, so I couldn't say he was this man or that man, and I feared that I might be called out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you also stated, at least the transcript that I read indicated you testified that this man had come earlier on. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I meant that he had come to the camp before. Maybe that's what I meant, something like that. When I heard his voice, I might have recognised him by his voice as being the same person who had come there before. But I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be provided with what has been marked as D26/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you look at this photograph, please. Earlier you were asked about this photograph in relation to those flower pots that you see in the photograph. I would like to ask you, looking at the people in that photograph, do you recognise the uniform that those people are wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my mind, that is the uniform of the civilian police. Dark trousers and a light blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when you testified that some of the guards at the Omarska camp wore the police uniform, the civilian police uniform, is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, I'd also like to ask you -- you may take that, please -- some additional questions about this pista area and how you defined the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: For those purposes, if the witness could be provided the exhibit which has been marked 3/82. It is a photograph of the model showing various buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, I wish to remind you that the witness identified on this exhibit what the pista was, but you may ask your question. But I think the witness has already told us that here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I have an additional question I'm going to ask in that regard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have testified, you have shown us what area it is that you defined as the pista. First of all, I would like you again to point to that area that you defined as the pista.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I call this area here [indicates] the pista. That's what I call the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, on Defence Exhibit 26/1, you were asked about some flower pots. Looking at this area you defined as the pista, can you show us, drawing a line, if you can, can you show us where these kinds of flower pots were placed on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the word "Zardinjera," flower pot. Oh, I see. I see. Here [indicates] and here [indicates], and there was some over there [indicates] too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You just pointed to a line that would be the hangar building and the restaurant building, on the side facing the "white house"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have just pointed to a line that would be from the hangar building to the restaurant building, on the side farthest away from the "white house"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also pointed to another area with flower pots, and where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some here [indicates] where the tap was, outside Mujo's room, in front of Mujo's dormitory. There was some water there, a tap, a water tap, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So the area that you have defined as the pista, the one between the restaurant building and the hangar building, you define the boundaries of the pista as those concrete flower pots; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have the witness provided with an exhibit I'm going to mark 3/87A and 3/87B, and these are English and B/C/S versions of the 1998 statement, the English version being "A" and the B/C/S version being 3/87B. Your Honour, I also have copies for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In my submission,

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: which have arisen out of cross-examination and which may be ambiguous. This witness was never presented with this statement at all during cross-examination, and there's no basis for showing it to him now. It's beyond the scope of cross-examination, and it's not appropriate for re-examination to explore these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's a bit disingenuous to say that this is beyond the scope of cross-examination. This witness was questioned on several occasions about what he had said in his 1998 statement. Now, the Defence didn't choose to show him that statement but they certainly brought the statement into issue. We submit that we have a right to not only question on that but to show him the statement they were using when questioning him, and we intend to offer it into evidence. So we believe that the objection is not well-founded and that we are well within our rights to present him with the statement and ask questions based on this statement, because on cross-examination, he was most certainly questioned about the 1998 statement and the 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have to overrule your objection, Mr. O'Sullivan. You know very well that almost all the statements given by the witness were discussed in the cross-examination. Therefore, we overrule your objection, and we ask Madam Hollis to continue with her re-examination. And we should like to have the exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Sir, in cross-examination you were asked about the procedure that was followed when this statement was taken, and you indicated that this same procedure was followed in taking this statement as was followed when your 1995 statement was taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was no pressure or anything like that. I gave my statement to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: When that statement was concluded, it was then read back to you in a language you understood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was read back to me, yes, without any problems, and I understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: And then you signed that statement and you also initialled certain pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you to look at the first page of this 1998 statement. Does your signature appear on that first page? Look at it in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: And then I would like you to look at pages 2 through 7 and tell us if your initials appear on those pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are my initials. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 8 and tell us whether your signature appears on that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does, up on top.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: I would like you to look at various portions of this statement in the B/C/S, so I will give both the cite in English and in the B/C/S version. First of all, I would like you to turn to page 3 in the B/C/S, that is also page 3 in the English, paragraph 5 in the B/C/S, which is paragraph 3 in the English. Now, on cross-examination, Defence counsel referred to a portion of what is found in that paragraph. I would like to refer to the entire paragraph. Sir, in that paragraph, it indicates: "That first night, when we got to the camp and were being searched and beaten, Kvocka was there. At the time when prisoners were being beaten and our personal possessions were seized, we had our heads bowed and instructions not to look around. Therefore, I cannot say Kvocka was standing close to us during our beating. However, as soon as the search and beating ended, we saw him. I am positive he saw each and every thing the guards did to us."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a correct statement. At that moment I didn't see him, but he was present there. It is correct. I didn't know him from before, but later, when he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, again, I would like you to look at page 3, the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S, on to page 4 in the B/C/S. And this is page 3, paragraph 5 in the English. And again, Defence counsel referred to a portion of this paragraph; I would like to refer to the entire paragraph. "On one such occasion I saw Kvocka speaking to a guard near the entrance of the restaurant. At that moment Zoran Zigic came and called out Asaf, Kiki, and Began. I don't know the names of Began and Kiki. Asaf and Began had restaurants in Prijedor, and Kiki had his own private business by the name of Kiki. As Zigic was calling out these names, guards said to the prisoners on the pista to lay on the floor facing the ground. Soon after we heard screams, and there was no way Kvocka could not have heard it. We were facing the floor for at least three hours, and during most of this time we could hear screams and cries coming from the direction of the 'white house.'" Now, is that what you said in your 1998 statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said that, but I also said that Kvocka went to the corner of the restaurant, and he could have prevented that. Whether that was the time when Zigic came -- but there was a case when I was in the restaurant. I don't remember these details, when he was talking and then leaving. Whether it was Zigic or one of the other guards, I can't remember now. I know he was present there when Zigic came and called out. But all the details -- where I was, when -- I can't say whether that was that particular moment or another moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm talking about the moment you have described to the Court. Now, I want to ask you: You, in this statement, use the name Zigic; in fact, you use the name Zoran Zigic. Now, how did you know that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the other detainees I heard the name. I still don't know his name, really. That man doesn't interest me at all. When he came, it was terrible. We all hid. I'd rather not talk about it. Because I personally didn't experience anything. I knew that he was coming, and I hid. He didn't touch me personally. I'm even afraid to think about it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that in this part of the proceedings we are talking at much greater length about Zigic than in the examination-in-chief, and we object and we appeal for a ruling. There are some statements here that are completely new, and we have no opportunity to respond to these statements, nor to the questions asked. I think that more is being said now about Zigic than during the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: First of all, there is nothing new here. It's in the statements that the Defence counsel have, so they could have examined about that. Secondly, Your Honour, the reason that I am asking about why he used the name in the statement is that I want the evidence to be clear for the Court that this witness did not know Zoran Zigic but that other people told him about it. The Prosecution believes that so the Court can adequately give weight to this witness' testimony, it's important that they understand that he did not know the name of this witness, and the reason it's in his statement is because he was repeating what others had told him. So it is for that reason that we were going into this. And in addition, Your Honour, part of this was read during the examination of this witness, and identification of Zigic, of course, was raised by the Defence. But we're not trying to bolster a positive identification; we are explaining, through this witness, to the Court, that indeed the witness never knew this man as Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief response, Your Honour. I should like to remind Your Honours that the statement referred to was not tendered into evidence. We drew attention to only a single sentence from that statement, and that is all. However, the statement, which is more than ten pages long, was not tendered into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you read a part of the statement. You opened doors. Each one of you, through the cross-examination, opens doors, and when you open such doors in the cross-examination, you are opening the door for the re-examination. You spoke about this. You're familiar with this rule, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I should have a chance for a replica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You mentioned this question. It is now up to the Prosecutor to clarify and to close the door you have opened. So we overrule your objection and we ask Madam Hollis to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: The next reference in this statement I would like to turn to is on page 4, paragraph 4, in the B/C/S; and it's page 4, paragraph 2, in the English. Now, during cross-examination, Defence counsel pointed out to you that during your testimony, you said that you never saw Kvocka enter the "white house." And then Defence counsel pointed out to you that in the 1998 statement you said that on many occasions you saw Kvocka enter the "white house." Now, you wanted to explain, but you were not given the opportunity to do that, so I would ask you to tell the Court what it was you wanted to explain about this difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to explain that I said that, but I personally didn't see him enter the "white house." He would go in that direction and then come back 10 or 15 minutes later. I didn't actually see him enter the "white house." I didn't want to go into those details. I didn't talk about that yesterday. I only want to talk about what I actually saw with my own eyes. I'd rather not talk about these other details. He went in that direction. Whether he was actually inside the "white house" or somewhere else, I couldn't follow. As far as he's concerned, he never did anything to me. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, again, referring to the statement, it would be page 2, paragraph 6 in the English; it would be the last paragraph on page 3, going on to page 4, in the B/C/S. In your 1998 statement you indicated: "I did not know Kvocka from before the war. I remember him introducing himself, saying, 'I am Kvocka and I am responsible for you.' This is how I learnt of him. Later other prisoners who recognised him told me he was Kvocka. He had married a Muslim, and his wife's brothers were also detained in the camp. I discovered all this later from his wife's neighbour, by the name of Amir Trta."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I learnt that, but I didn't see her brothers, I didn't know them, so I didn't want to go into any other details. This is all hearsay. I heard this, and that is what I said. I'm only saying what I really knew. I didn't know Kvocka in person, or his brothers-in-law, so I didn't go into those details.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, I would ask that the witness be actually shown again the copy of the exhibit that was marked D25/1. If the witness would look at the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you indicated that the procedure for taking this statement was the same as in 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you would look at that statement, and tell us, looking at page 1 of that statement, does your signature appear on page 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: If you would look at page 2, do your initials appear on page 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, about the Zeljko, the name Zeljko, and above that, my initials.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, do your initials appear as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: On page 3, does your signature appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My signature, initials are there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave that 1995 statement, did you answer the questions that were asked of you, to the best of your memory at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I started talking, then they asked me questions, then when I remembered I would say. Because now, sitting here, I sometimes think of things that I didn't say when I was interviewed. But I just want to say that I only am answering what I actually do know. I don't want to go into these minute details.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: In 1998 did you answer the questions that were asked of you, based on the best of your memory at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked if you ever heard Kvocka give orders to kill anyone, and you said no, you did not. Did you ever hear Kvocka order the guards or other people in the camp not to kill detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that either.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Kvocka order the guards or other people in the camp to stop abusing detainees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Witness. Mr. Simic has an objection to make. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, objection, Your Honour. The witness gave a decisive answer to that question when he was asked it, when he was asked whether he had seen Mr. Kvocka ever order anybody anything, and especially with respect to abuse. And Witness AI said -- he didn't say -- he said he didn't hear Mr. Kvocka give out any orders, and I think it is a tendentious question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, perhaps we can wait to hear what the next question is from Madam Hollis. We're repeating everything the witness said. Sometimes we repeat the witness' answer to be able to ask a question, so let's wait and see what Madam Hollis' question is. Madam Hollis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What I would note, Your Honour, that what I saw in the transcript was to the effect that he never heard Kvocka give any orders to do harm. I'm asking if he ever heard Kvocka give orders not to do harm. I believe it is opened by the prior question, and I believe it is a different question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever hear Kvocka intervene to stop any abuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, you testified about one occasion when a man came and he was calling aloud names of detainees and Kvocka was present. Did you hear or see anything to indicate that Kvocka questioned that man about who he was or why he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said they did not meet at that particular moment. Whether they talked or not later on somewhere, I didn't see, so -- when this man came, the other man left.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: You were asked why -- you were asked if you ever complained about your beatings, and you indicated that you did not complain. Why did you not complain about these beatings you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I were to complain, I thought that I would be treated even worse, so I didn't dare complain to anybody. That was the reason. I didn't dare. I always tried to hide, out of fear. I was just afraid to complain.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: And why did you feel that if you complained you would be treated even worse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have the feeling that the guard would be removed. I thought the guard would exert even greater pressure on me, and that's why I didn't dare complain.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, these beatings that you received, were these beatings that were out in the open or were you taken away to some private place and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly it was out in the open. On my way to the restaurant, Drazenko would hit me. He did so on the pista too. But I wasn't ever called out and taken to a special room; just in these parts. What he had against me, this Drazen, whom I didn't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned during cross-examination a man named Slavko, and you said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of his answer. We didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said, "This is Slavko," and allegedly he had taken part in the attack on Prijedor. I don't know this man at all. And he was allegedly in the Green Berets. They used to cry "Ustasha." But I wasn't interested in that. I was afraid, so I didn't pay attention to whether it was Slavko or not. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: Now, this man that they said, "This is Slavko," where was it that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on the pista, and I saw him from the pista. He was brought to us. Where he was brought from, I don't know. I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: What was his condition when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was beaten up. His face was all swollen, as far as I was able to see at that moment. But I didn't know the man and I never differentiated between Catholics, Muslims, Orthodox. I didn't know what he was, whether he was an Orthodox or a Serb or a Croat, or whatever. That wasn't important to me. If we were friends, we were friends. I wasn't interested in that kind of thing at all, and that's the same kind of thing I do now.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: You also were questioned about what happened when you were lying face down on the pista, and then you indicated at some point you saw Kiki, when this incident occurred when he and Began and the others were called out. Now, if you were lying face down on the pista, how were you able to see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you move a little bit, and I happened to move a bit and saw what I saw. You raise your head up a bit, that kind of thing. That's how it was. And if -- but if the guards saw you move and take a look, then he would walk across us and beat us until he got to that particular person, so that we did this sort of secretly.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION IS LIMITED
utterances.text: You were asked about the decision to terminate you from your employment, and you were asked if you appealed that. You said you did not appeal that. Why did you not appeal that decision to terminate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said: I had come out of the camp. It was from fear that I would not be returned. So I went home, I talked to my father, asked him what he thought I should do. He said, "Well, stay here. We've got enough food and money." And when this disappeared, he said, "Well let's get the papers together." And I couldn't, because my children didn't have anything to eat, so I had to leave Prijedor. And had I not left, I don't know what would have happened, because I didn't have anything to live on. I had no means of livelihood, no food, no money.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. Have you got something important? Because it's time for the Judges' questions, as you know full well, at this point. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind that Madam Hollis left the door slightly ajar, I should like to ask you to enable me to ask only two questions in regard to what Madam Hollis brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Identify the door, please, Mr. Simic. What door would you like to open? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis spoke about the possibility of Kvocka hearing this, and I'd just like to clarify that question, and the question related to the orders. Just two brief questions, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is it's a follow-on to the questions that he asked, so we don't think we're opening any doors. But if Your Honours feel it would assist you, we certainly have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As there are no objections on the side of the Prosecution, and even if there are the Trial Chamber feels that there are rules to follow, but what we are interested in is arriving at the truth and the whole truth. So we're going to authorise you to put your questions, but be quick, please, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I should like to express my gratitude, Your Honour. To speed up things, I shall be asking them from this position here and not come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Simic:

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AI, on several occasions you said today that you only wish to speak about what you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In connection to Ms. Hollis' question and the transcript, please answer the following: Do you know whether Mr. Kvocka heard what you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he was in the building, if we heard them, he could hear them too. And I would see him five or ten minutes previously. He had to hear, as far as I'm concerned, just in the same way that we heard them. He had to hear voices, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: And if he was in a closed premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he could have heard too, because I was inside and I heard what was going on, so he must have heard too.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: My second question linked to the orders. Did you ever see Mr. Kvocka issuing any orders whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I have already said that. No. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection. Just to clear something up, and it is a matter of interpretation. When I receive the B/C/S interpretation, it says that Madam Hollis, who asked her question as she should have, that is to say, whether the witness was beaten publicly or whatever, and it turned out that Madam Hollis was asking in the plural, whether "they" beat him, which means several people, in the plural. That is the interpretation I got into Serbian. And the witness is clearly speaking about one man, saying that one man beat him and that only one man -- he was beaten by only one man. I don't know what the interpretation will be like in French, so I'd like to clarify that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's position is I think ultimately you need to look at the transcript. The Prosecution's recollection of the transcript is that the witness said that it was mostly Predojevic who beat him, "mostly." Not that it was only Predojevic, but mostly. Again, I think we're getting into areas here that are differences of recollection on the transcript, and the transcript should be definitive. But anyway, the Prosecution's recollection is that he never said it was only Predojevic but that it was mostly Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you have any objections to the fact that Madam Hollis can repeat the question and hear the witness' answer again?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no objections to make. I just say that there are differences in the interpretation. To our answers, he said in Serbian in the singular. Madam Hollis heard something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask Madam Hollis, could you please repeat the question. Put it to the witness again and we're going to record the answer, now that we're all here, and we're going to pay attention to this. Madam Hollis, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a question about the beatings, in the plural, that you received while you were in the Omarska camp. The question is: Did these beatings, in the plural, did these beatings occur in public areas, or were you taken away to some private area for these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several beatings when I went to get food; more than one guard beat at that time. Drazenko Predojevic beat me especially, but I got it from other guards too. Depending on how I would pass them by, I would either be beaten once or five or six times, depending on your luck. And so those beatings were when we went to get food. I didn't go to get food often because I was sick and so on, all the things that happened to me afterwards, because I was afraid of the beatings. But personally Drazenko did it most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: These beatings you referred to when you went to get food were in public areas, is that correct, areas where other people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Thirty of us would be going in a column, and they would be at the corridor and they would start to beat us until we got our food. So it depends who got what in passing. You might get more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that clear now, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear, Mr. President, that there is a difference between to beat and to beat up, or to inflict blows and to beat. The Defence maintains that Drazenko beat him, but here, the 30 of them were going by and they would receive the odd blow. So there's a difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, I think that that goes beyond the conditions that the witness has described. We, of course, are all intelligent individuals and we know the consequences of this. But thank you anyway, Mr. Fila. To round off that question, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity, and I apologise to my colleague, Judge Riad, I'm going to ask the question: Are you able to identify the people, the persons, who beat you, apart from Drazenko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not able. I have a face in my mind, Drazenko, his face. But everything was very fast, go and take the food, get it back, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for the moment. I give the floor to Judge Fouad Riad. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness AI, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a few questions to ask you perhaps to help me understand more clearly certain points which came in your testimony. The first question which I'd like you to try to clarify is how you could reconcile, really, two things which you mentioned: One, which you repeated, especially when you were cross-examined by Mr. Fila, that prisoners were beaten at random according to the whim of the guard, of the guardians or the prison keepers; and at the same time, when you were in the interrogation room and this guard wanted to hit you, they ordered him not to hit you, while another one, who is Sefik, went into the interrogation room and came out -- was carried out beaten to death. So in fact there was somebody in control, somebody who could tell them, "Don't hit. Don't kill," otherwise they wouldn't have stopped beating you in the interrogation room. What was your assessment in that case? Was there a higher authority that could decide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am able to understand, there was someone there to decide. But when they were interrogating me, I don't know who actually interrogated me, but they might have known my parents, for example, according to my statements that I wasn't guilty, and I'd already lost quite a lot of weight so he probably said, "Don't beat him" because I was telling the truth, so perhaps that is the reason why he didn't allow the other person to beat me, depending on who was being interrogated at that time. So I don't know the reason, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you for the reason. But there could be someone saying, "Don't beat. Stop."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. At that particular moment, it was that person interrogating me who said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, speaking about the discipline, you mentioned that the guards came in in a line and the superiors were standing on the side. So did it look like a disciplined prison or camp, or was it something out of any order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon arrival it looked as if there was some discipline in this order and that somebody did have some authority over the guards, as far as I was able to make out at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You even said that upon arrival there was no beating, and then after that, in the cross-examination, you said that you were beaten and you were searched. I think in the cross-examination with Mr. Simic you said that Kvocka was present when you arrived and you were beaten and you were searched. Is that right? So you were beaten when you arrived and you were searched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in my bus, no beating, but maybe the other bus. Perhaps I explained this in a different way. Me personally, nobody beat me, but when the other bus came, they did. Who was there, whether Kvocka or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No. You said that Kvocka was present in this case when there was beating. Is that right, or I understood wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that person. I saw him when I got there, and then he introduced himself, when we were supposed to go into the dormitory. So that person was there in that compound. I didn't know him before that. I heard that people had been beaten but I didn't see that. So he must have known. He could not have suddenly turned up and left again. So he was in that circle. But I didn't know him personally so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And then you knew afterwards that it was Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he introduced himself, then I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you also said that he did not do any beating by himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't see that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not beat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you noticed that he was a person of authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because that's how he introduced himself, that he was the chief there and that everything would be okay. He introduced himself. He wasn't terrible in any way, so as far as he's concerned, I haven't got a bad opinion about him, as concerns myself, towards me, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you what he did. He did not give any order to stop. He did not beat but he did not give any order to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't. Had he given that order, it would have stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He would have had the authority to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the way he introduced himself, he did have. Whether there was anybody above him, I can't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. I mean, when he was there, was there somebody above him at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that there was anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also concerning the same thing, concerning Mr. Kvocka, you said when you were sitting in the pista, I won't repeat what you said, Kvocka was close to the man calling the names and he turned afterwards and went to the restaurant, or something, and he could hear, he could hear the cries of the people being beaten. Did I understand you rightly? And he did not interfere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He did not interfere. He went away from the entrance where he was standing, but I don't think he left the building. Perhaps he went outside the camp. I don't know. I didn't see him any more. But if he was present there, then he had to have heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But he had nothing to do with the man calling the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see that they met and had an agreement of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, apparently Mr. Drazenko Predojevic was the man giving you this hard time. Was there anything between you and him, or did he apply this to everybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He beat others mostly too, but he beat me mostly because of my shoes, because I had those worker's boots, or perhaps the guard who took me to interrogation and came back and told me, "You'll pay for that." I don't know. I don't know why, actually. I didn't know him personally so I don't actually know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And there was no chance of complaining to the higher authorities. You were completely at his mercy. Because, as you said, at the interrogation room you were protected and somebody protected from that, so nobody could protect you from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, possibly they could have but I didn't dare complain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Mr. Krkan, Krkan's shift was the most cruel, and that he was there from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 at night. So in a way, he could see completely what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Fila, but I don't think we ought to interrupt at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there. He had to have known what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was he also on a higher grade? Did he look like also, as you mentioned about Kvocka, that he was the head of this division and he could exert orders on them in any form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was under Kvocka, a lower position, but he was superior to the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you saw him giving orders to the guards in any form and being obeyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see him issue anything, but I saw him walking around with the guards, talking to them. Now, whether he issued orders for beatings of any kind, I can't say I heard that. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, he did not issue orders for beating. But he did not issue orders for not beating, never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, concerning Krle, you said that you saw him shooting the man before your eyes. Was this man trying to run away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was something wrong with his nerves. He had a sort of breakdown. Krle told him to sit down, and then afterwards he jumped out of the "white house." What happened, I don't know. But Krle's shift was one of the best, and I was surprised that that happened then, that is to say, the best, they beat less. So I was surprised to see that because a couple of times I asked him if I could go to the toilet and he let me, so this was a surprise for me, this reaction. Who knows what he thought at that moment and what actually went on and what actually happened. I don't know. But that's what happened, that's all I can say, as far as I was able to see myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it customary for anybody trying to run away to be shot? Did you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was the first time that I saw this shooting and a man killed. It was the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did see it clearly. You saw it clearly. You were at enough distance to know what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was where I was. And I saw the man get up. First of all he told him to sit down. Then he took him to the "white house." And they were waiting for a shift to turn up. At that point the man might have jumped out and moved towards the pista and the shot was fired. I don't know the reasons. That's what I saw. That's what I saw happening. Before that, the man cried out, "Stop" to the other one, he didn't stop, and then that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a convenient time to break. Judge Wald has some questions, I do too, but I think we'll have a 30-minute recess and resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald, please. Just a moment, please. Please be seated. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness AI, you testified, I believe, that Mr. Kvocka addressed the group of detainees on the first evening that you were at Omarska. My question to you is: When he did that, did he in any way identify his own role or position in the camp? I think that when you answered Judge Riad's question you said, "He said he was chief," but earlier you said that he said he was responsible for them. And I just want to clarify exactly how he identified his role when he addressed you that evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he was responsible for us, so this would imply that he was camp commander or a chief. If he says that he is responsible for us, then that means that he is the main person there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Was that the only time during your stay at Omarska that any camp official addressed the entire group or a large group of detainees, or were there other occasions when other camp officials or Mr. Kvocka again addressed large groups of detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was the only one who addressed us, introducing himself by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said, I believe, that things tended to be better around the camp for the detainees when the interrogators were there, the ones that came in the morning and left at 5.00. I was wondering how that could be so if so much of the beatings took place on the way to get meals, which you told us happened during the daytime. Maybe you could help me understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If somebody came from the outside, he wouldn't come during the working hours of the interrogators, and there were fewer call-outs. That's what I was talking about. But the blows as we went to eat, these were happening all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In your experience at Omarska, did you ever hear cries or see people coming out of the interrogation rooms, the daytime interrogations, that looked like or sounded like they were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear noise up there, cries. And when they came out, one would see them covered in blood, and I saw one neighbour going up there and he was carried out of there. So what exactly happened in there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: After the -- thank you. After the interrogators that came from outside the camp and left at the end of the day left, and when people were called out at night, was that supposedly -- were they told they were being called out for interrogations, or did everybody know it was just a call-out for beatings? When the call-outs came at night, what did everybody think or know the reason for the call-outs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they would tell you to take your things with you, that would mean that you would be taken somewhere outside the camp. And if it was just to come out, then we knew it was beatings. So that if you were told to take your things, you knew you wouldn't come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. At one point in your testimony you said there were three groups in the camp; there were the outside unit of police which left after -- a special police which left after, I think it was, a few weeks; there were the guards which you said included both military and army police; and then you said there was the army. Now, this third group, this third group, the army, were they -- they didn't do guard duty? What did they do around the camp, this third group that you referred to as the army? Were they separate from the guards, and what functions did they perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say "the army," I meant a guard wearing a uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, and if he was a wearing a blue uniform he was a policeman. So maybe there was a misunderstanding. I was just referring to the uniforms the guards were wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That helps clarifies it, but just to pin it down. In other words, there were people wearing regular army uniforms who were in the guard shifts; right? Is that right? Who were part of the guard shifts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question to you is: At any time when you were there, were you ever told that -- or did you ever learn that there were certain times or certain shifts where you weren't supposed to talk or you must be much more quiet than normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew amongst ourselves that if Krkan's shift was on duty, and it was one of the worst, so amongst ourselves we agreed to keep quiet. Nobody told us, but we were more fearful than otherwise at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness AI, I have a few questions too. Are you able to repeat a conversation using the same words, the words that Kvocka used when he introduced himself? Are you able to quote him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I'm not sure whether he uttered his name. He said, "I am 'something' Kvocka. I am responsible for you while you are here. You will be interrogated and everything will be all right and then you will be spent back home." That is what he said to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We now have the words, more or less. Another question. You mentioned when the shifts changed, next to the line of guards was the guard leader, on the side. Was he at that moment giving orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. But when he reached a certain guard post, the other guard would take over. I didn't notice them exchanging any words. I just saw them changing places. I didn't hear anyone saying "You go there," "You go here," or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, you spoke either of Krkan or Krle or Kvocka who were moving around a little, at least you watched them move about in relation to a particular place, or did they move all around the camp? Was there a difference, or did the same apply to Krkan, Krle, and Kvocka? Was there any difference in their movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They moved around normally. They would tour the compound. I saw them walking around, not any particular position. They would go upstairs, to the premises above the restaurant, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the bodies that you saw behind the "white house" and next to the red building, did Krkan, Krle, or Kvocka, while walking around the camp, could they see those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those next to the "white house," they could have seen, as we saw them from the pista. Also if they went up close down there, they could have seen them. I only saw them when I went to urinate there. It depended on which position they held at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the "white house," where was the entrance to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the direction of the hangar, the pista there and then the hangar. So it depended where you sat on the pista. If you were on the side, then you could see those bodies, if you were on that same side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, considering where you are now and where I am, the entrance in relation to the model that we have between us, the main gate, was it on your side or on my side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my side, the main gates to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please get up and point out the main entrance to the camp, with the help of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness is a protected witness, so it is not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for drawing my attention to that point. So the main entrance to the camp was on your side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the people who were entering and coming out of the camp did not pass by the "white house."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but it may assist you if, perhaps, the witness were shown 3/82, that's a photo of the model, and then he could perhaps point to where you would like him to point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's a very good suggestion. Thank you. Could you put that exhibit on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher. Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Witness, could you please point to the main entrance on that exhibit for us, the main entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here [indicates], in this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the side of the restaurant building. It was through that gate that you entered the camp in the bus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see it. Yes, but that is where I got off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. Thank you. Another question. How many people were in the bus that brought you to the Omarska camp? You have already given an answer to Mr. Simic, saying that there were between 40 and 50. Let me put the question differently. The bus, did it have more persons than sitting space, or was there one person to each seat, or one seat to each person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I think we were all sitting. It was a bus belonging to the public transportation system, so that is why I said there were between 40 and 50. I was in the fifth or sixth row, and I was sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were not in a position to see the people who searched you, but you said that you heard them speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't see them, yes, but I heard them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the search and during your stay in the camp, did you hear that voice or those voices again or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment I was afraid, so I didn't pay much attention. I may have heard a similar voice later but I can't claim that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. On the 30th of May, 1992, you were sitting on the pista. How much time did you spend in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was already nightfall. It became cool when they moved us to Mujo's room. I don't know what time it was, but it was getting cooler, and we were moved inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to go back with you to the semicircular glassed-in entrance to the restaurant. Was Krkan there always, or did he move away from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He moved around, as I said. He didn't have any particular post. All of those leaders of the camp moved around. They didn't have a particular position to hold. I never saw them in one place all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During your stay at the Omarska camp, did anyone visit you from the outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not me personally. But there was a colleague of mine from work; whether he came to look for somebody or not, I didn't call his attention to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But generally speaking, did anybody visit the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one from the International Red Cross came to visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I heard that a journalist had come but I wasn't there to see them. I was in the hangar at the time so I didn't see anyone. Whether they came or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Witness AI, you have just completed your testimony here at the International Criminal Tribunal. We thank you very much, and we hope that you will be able to recover from your suffering. You may now leave, and we thank you very much. I think the blinds have to be pulled down, Mr. Usher, the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all, Your Honours, if I have been of any assistance. Maybe it will make my life easier too later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis or Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we deal with the exhibits at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May be deal with the exhibits at this time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right, Ms. Hollis. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution would offer the following exhibits into evidence: Exhibits 3/80A and B, those were photographs showing vehicles, including what were identified as police vehicles; 3/81, a picture of individuals in what were described as regular camouflage uniforms, including the man identified as Drljaca; 3/82, which is a photograph of the model of Omarska; 3/37, which was a previously marked exhibit which had been filed with the Chamber but was not offered into evidence, that was a photograph of the truck that was identified as the type of truck that carried the dead bodies; 3/83, which was a photograph of the portion of the administration building with the circular portion and the glass facing toward the pista and the hangar, and the witness made annotations on that exhibit; 3/84A through D, that was the photo board exhibit, the composite exhibit dealing with the accused Kvocka, "A" being the notice of procedures, "B" being the interpreter's certification, "C" being the report, and "D" being the copy of the photo board; 3/85A through Delta1, A through D1, this was the composite exhibit of the photo board display dealing with Krle, "A" being the notice of procedures, "B" being the interpreter's certification, "C" being the report, "D" and "D1" being the photo boards. Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would also stipulate that the third photo array shown to the witness contained the photograph of accused Zigic and that the witness indicated he did not recognise anyone on that photo array. Your Honours, the Prosecution further offers into evidence 3/86A and B, being the decision on termination of employment of this witness, "A" being the English and "B," the B/C/S. We also offer 3/87A and B, that being the 18 September 1998 Office of the Prosecutor statement taken of Witness AI, "A" being the English and "B" being the B/C/S. The Prosecution would give notice to the Court at this time that if the Defence does not introduce into evidence what has been marked D25/1, that is, the 1995 statement of Witness AI, the Prosecution wishes to offer that into evidence as a Prosecution Exhibit. At this moment, those are the exhibits we would move admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, are you going to speak on behalf of all counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I speak in my own name. Your Honour, there are two points: First of all, a question that the Defence feels needs to be addressed, and that is showing the witness what they said previously. With all due respect for Judge Riad, he said to the witness that he had said that Krkan's shift was the cruelest. I looked through the transcript and I didn't find that statement. So my first question is what are the possibilities of the Defence to respond in view of Article 5 and Rule 85? This is being repeated several times. That is the first issue. The second has to do with the exhibit tendered by my learned friend Ms. Hollis, regarding 3/87A and B. This is the statement of Witness AI of the 18th of September, 1998. As you know, Mr. President, in the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution did not use that statement. In the cross-examination, by some Defence counsel it was mentioned but not by me. I have no objection that it be admitted as evidence in relation to Defence counsel who did refer to it. I think it is not fair that what others do should apply to me. I did not open that door, and I move that if that evidence is admitted that all mention of the accused Mladjo Radic be redacted from it, because I didn't refer to it in the cross-examination; it was not mentioned in the examination-in-chief. It is not fair and my Defence will be prejudiced if the consequences of the examination by other Defence counsel are imposed upon me. Therefore, the parts in which Mladjo Radic is mentioned should be redacted. And I wish to underline that Ms. Hollis did not use that statement with reference to Mladjo Radic, not even after the cross-examination by the Defence. She did not mention it in the examination-in-chief, nor in the re-examination. So it is a specific situation, and I would like that part of the statement to be redacted. Otherwise, the rights of the accused to a fair trial would be in jeopardy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, we have heard well, but this was not the moment for you to speak. When you stood on your feet and I gave you the floor, I thought you were speaking on behalf of the Defence. The rule is to give the floor to the Defence in the order of the indictment, so it's Mr. Simic who should speak first. But in any event, regarding the first point, I have to respond in the way I have already done: The transcript speaks for itself and it will show whether the witness said or did not say what Judge Riad repeated. Another point is that you may draw conclusions about this at the end and you can bring witnesses to deny this, and anyway you can also appeal. But in any event it is not possible to interrupt the Judges when they are asking questions, and that is something that I have to tell you now, Mr. Fila, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the only point I wanted to make is that there is no grounds in the Rule for my objection -- and you're quite right, there's no question about that -- but I don't know how to deal with it. Because if you say to the witness, "You said so and so" and he says yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, you always have the transcript and you can prove that the witness did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but then it's too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I for a moment. I was listening to the English translation, and I noted that the witness said that he avoided going to the toilet so as not to be beaten by the guards, and above all that they were fiercest under Krkan's shift. He said this when talking about going to the toilet because during that time it was worse, the situation was worse. If I am wrong, I apologise, and if that is the case -- but if I am right, I should like the attorney to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but the difference is something else. The question referred to going to lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, there is a second side to your intervention, Mr. Fila, which we will treat together after we hear the comments by other Defence. In any event, thank you for your remarks. Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have already said that we should like to tender into evidence the statement of 1995, D25/1, and on this occasion we should like, as the Defence, with regard to the inconsistencies of statements, would like to tender the 18th of September statement, 3/87A and B, because this statement was taken by the same interviewer one month after the Kvocka interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Simic, do I understand you correctly, you have no objection to the tendering into evidence of the exhibits that Madam Hollis asked to be tendered and admitted into evidence; is that right? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. We propose them too, and we do not object to them, or the other proposals either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Nikolic, will it be Mr. O'Sullivan who will be taking the floor? That's just what I wanted to know. Thank you. So Mr. O'Sullivan has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In regards to admission of exhibits, without commenting or detracting from the objection of Mr. Fila, we have no objection to the admissibility of the exhibits.
